newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa launches population policy debate.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa launches population policy debate.

text.p: The South African government on Monday published a draft programme to cut population growth but without the controversial targets set by the previous white government.

Successive white governments tried a number of ways to limit black population growth and to promote white fertility, causing cynicism in black society about family planning initiatives seen by some as scientific genocide.

"We have taken a very complex and different approach. It doesn't set targets. It doesn't focus on just one dimension of the problem," Director General of Welfare Leila Patel told a parliamentary committee.
"South Africa needs an explicit, comprehensive and multi- sectoral population policy."

The document highlights the wide disparity in black and white living conditions, mortality and fertility and predicts a doubling in the estimated 40 to 43.5 million population in 32 years if population growth does not decline more quickly.

The overall population growth rate dropped from six percent a year in 1950 to four percent in 1990, but the black majority - estimated in the policy paper at 77.5 percent of the population - continues to outstrip whites, who make up 12.1 percent of the total population.
"The contraceptive prevalence rate is highest among whites at 81 percent in 1994 and lowest among Africans at 55 percent. It is also higher in metropolitan than in rural areas," the document said.
Several committee members, mostly black women, said the policy paper would have to offer more specific ideas to empower rural black women to control and plan family size.
The document lists 24 strategies for population development, ranging from improved data collection and analysis to inter- departmental coordination of legislation.
It identifies poverty as "one of the most formidable enemies of choice" and highlights the need to take appropriate medical services to rural women.
It calls for equality between men and women in all aspects of family life, including housekeeping, and urges "population education" in schools.
But the document makes no suggestions on how to educate people on family planning and does not address the distribution of contraceptives or access to sterilisation.
The infant mortality rate among blacks dropped from 166 per 1,000 live births in 1950 to 51 in 1990, but remains almost six times the white rate of nine deaths per 1,000 live births.
